articles.text: As will be seen by our market report, the prices on Texas cattle have risen twenty-five cents and shipping and dressed beef cattle have risen ten to fifteen cents. Montana cattle sold at $4.75 and Oregon cattle at $4.85.

articles.text: Several train-loads of cattle have gone east during the week. We wish we were in a position to protest to some purpose to the shipping of some of the cattle. The most of them were in fair to good condition, but every car-load was disfigured by scalawags that there was no profit whatever in shipping. They would certainly bring down the price of the bunch more than they are worth.
articles.summary: Several trainloads of cattle went east during the week; the editor objects to shipping inferior 'scalawag' cattle with them.

articles.text: The only resource for the Indian lease cattlemen to get rid of their catile is to send them to market. This will have to be done with at least 200,000 head. It behooves our cowmen to watch this narrowly, as the putting on the market of this immense number of cattle inside of thirty days, will bring the price way down. Dakota and Montana cattle striking the market at that time will suffer seriously in the general depression.
articles.summary: Warns that forced marketing of some 200,000 head from Indian lease lands will depress prices for Dakota and Montana cattle.

articles.text: The Colorado brand law is now in force. It possesses many good points that should be embodied in a statute that can easily be passed at the next session of the Dakota legislature. The Colorado law provides that the state brand-book shall be in the possession of the secretary of state. Every person or corporation owning live stock in the state by August 1, must have forwarded his or their brands to the secretary. After Aug. 1, any new brand must be forwarded to the secretary who will record the same provided it is not already recorded. The secretary will forward to the owner a certified copy of the record, when the brand shall also be recorded in the offices of the clerk or recorder of the county or counties in which the stock will range. It shall be unlawful for any county officer to record a brand not authorized by the secretary of state. The brand, properly recorded, becomes personal property and can be sold or traded as such. The secretary of state must publish the state brand-book ninety days after Aug. 1, for general distribution.
articles.summary: Summarizes Colorado's new state brand law and urges the Dakota legislature to adopt similar provisions.

articles.headline: County Organization.
articles.text:
A number of persons have lately spoken to us and in fact the burden of the conversation seems to be the advisability of organizing the county. This is by no means confined to Medora alone, but at least half the stockmen in the county have voluntarily expressed their wish that the county be organized provided it does not cost an unreasonable amount.

In conversation with sheriff Harmon, of Morton Co., our eyes were opened on the subject of expenses. The actual running expenses of a county are about as follows: $300 each to the recorder and treasurer, $150 to the county attorney, $100 to the assesor, and $3 each per day to the commissioners while in actual session. The sheriff's fees will surely fall short of $1,000. This will make the running expenses of the county not over $2,000. In addition to this, a good set of county books will cost about $1,2[00?] and rent of buildings for county offices, say $600. This will make the expenses for the first year in the neighborhood of $4,000. Of this amount, at least $3,600 and perhaps more will be obtained from the railroad, leaving less than $400 to be raised from the county.

Is there a man in the county after this showing, who does not want to organize? More than this, if we organize before the tax is collected by Stark Co., we do not need to pay a cent to that county. Sheriff Harmon says that this fact is proved beyond a doubt.

Even if the organization cost the people of Billings Co., $4,000 instead of $400 we think there would be no unwillingness to organize.

With official power a hundred and fifty miles away, life and property are not safe. Who would object to paying his share of $400 or even $4,000 to secure protection?

An easy problem for each to solve is to figure the total assessable property at $500,000. Then say even $4,000 had to be raised. This would equal a tax of eight mills. Now figure yonr share and see if protection to life and property is not worth the price. After figuring your share of $4,000, consider that the tax is liable to be only one-tenth of that original amount and see if it is profitable to be at the mercy of any drunken ruffian who wants to paint the town red.

All the above figuring does not include the subject of licenses. Medora is now paying Morton Co. $1,200 per yeer for license tax. This amount will pay all the school and road expenses of the county.

To conclude, we think that there is scarcely anyone in the county opposed to organization. All it rednires is a little effort in getting the signatures and the thing is done. We have sworn off on plans for organization and propose to let others "run the masheen." We do not ask for nor want any office whatever but propose to be entirely free to criticize any move we see fit.

Stockmen should see that it is for their interest and themselves start the ball rolling.
articles.summary: Editorial urging the organization of Billings County, citing Sheriff Harmon's estimate that first-year costs would be about $4,000, mostly covered by railroad taxes.

articles.headline: Cow Boy Dictionary.
articles.text:
Our first issue of the cow-boy dictionary attracted much attention and a large number took enough interest in it to offer additions and corrections. Our thanks in this direction are especially due to C. R. Kelsey, of Glendive and Rassie Deffebach. We hope that as much interest will be felt in this issue, and corrections and additions sent or handed us as before. Our next issue will contain an addenda, with all the corrections and additions handed us.

P

Paunch, v. t. To shoot through the paunch any cattle that are hard to drive. It sickens them temporarily and makes them docile.

Pen, v. t. To drive animals into a corrall or enclosure,

Picket-pin, n. An iron or wooden stake driven into the ground to hold a horse, tied to it with a rope.

Picket-rope, n. A rope used to tie up horses.

Pilgrim, n. Referring to cattle, means an animal new to a country. A tenderfoot.

Pinto, adj. An animal spotted with large white and bay spots. A calico-horse.

Pitch, v.t. See buck.

Q

Quarter-breed, n. A man or animal having one-fourth white or pure blood.

Quirt, n. A short cow-boy whip usually with loaded handle and two leather thongs for lashes.

R

Ranch, n. A cow-camp dwelling-house.

Ranch-brand, n. A brand used on animals after they are on the owner's range.

Range, n. The territory over which cattle graze.

Range-cattle, n. See grass-cattle.

Range-riding, v. t. To ride over the range, looking after the welfare of cattle.

Reata, n. A rawhide lasso.

Remoutha, n. A bunch of saddle horses.

Riding-circle, v. t. To ride on the out-skirts of a round-up party driving all cattle into the round-up bunch.

Rig, adj. Denoting the kind. Generally used with reference to saddles. Ex. Double-rigged saddle, meaning double-cinch saddle.

Ring-bit, n. A cow-boy bridle-bit with ring extending entirely around the lower jaw.

Rope, n. General word for lasso, reata, couresta, grass-rope &c.

Round-up, v. t. The act of driving all animals in a district into a bunch or bunches, for purposes of branding, reclaiming, or shipping.

Round-up, adj. Referring to the party or outfit on a cattle-gathering expedition.

Running-brand, n. A brand made with a running iron.

Running-iron, n. A branding-iron consisting of an iron rod with a bend in the end like a fish-hook.

Rustle, v. i. To be wide awake to opportunities of advancement.

Rustle, v. t. To steal.

Rustler, n. 1. A wide-awake energetic man. 2. A thief, usually a horse-thief.

S

Saddle-iron, n. Short branding-iron to be carried on the saddle.

Shack, n. 1. A horse's gait, between a walk and a trot. 2. A cheap western dwelling.

Single-foot, n. A horse's gait, resembling pacing or racking, except that one foot is placed on the ground at a time.

Slicker, n. A water-proof coat, made of strong porous cloth, saturated with oil.

Sombrero, n. A light-colored, broad-brimmed, cow-boy hat.

Spade-bit, n. A cow-boy bridle bit, with a spade-like extension of the bit toward the throat.

Split, n. An ear-mark signifying ownership, made by cutting the ear from the middle to the tip.

Squaw-trot, n. Slow run. Favorite gait of Indians and hunters.

Stock-inspector, n. An officer appointed by a cattlemen's association, to oversee all sales of cattle, with authority to rectify any illegal proceedings.

String, n. The bunch of horses ridden by one man.

String-team, n. Horses or mules hitched in pairs, one after another. Sometimes there are thirty or more animals hitched in this way.

Swallow-fork, n. An ear-mark signifying ownership, made by cutting a v-shaped piece from the ear, the apex being in the middle of the ear and the ends at the tip.

T

Tailing, v. t. Throwing down cattle by the tail, after being lassoed and heeled. Holding cattle down when thrown, by pulling on the tail passed between the animal's hind legs.

Tapideros, n. Leather coverings for stirrups, used by cow-boys for protection to the feet.

Tenderfoot, n. A stranger, ignorant of western ways.

Tepee, n. An Indian lodge, made of poles and skin or bark.

Texas-fever, n. A kind of disease, insufficiently diagnosed, which southern Texas cattle communicate to other cattle, usually terminating fatally. The disease is contagious but harmless to the southern Texas cattle themselves. The disease is often called splenetic fever.

Texas-trail, n. The trail made and used by Texas cattle being driven to the northern ranges.

Thorough-bred, adj. Referring to a horse descended from pure Arabian animals.

Throat-latch, n. The strap extending around the neck to keep the bridle in place.

Through-cattle, n. Cattle driven from one range to another a long distance away. Usually referring to Texas cattle driven to northern ranges.

Trail, v. t. To drive cattle over a trail, usually referring to the Texas trail.

Trail, n. A path worn by men or animals.

Trail-brand, n. A brand used on animals while on the trail.

Trail-cattle, n. Cattle driven over a trail, usually referring to the Texas trail.

Trail-cinch, n. The hind cincha on a saddle.

Trail-herd, n. See trail-cattle.

Travois, n. A kind of vehicle made by strapping the ends of two poles to the sides of a horse and allowing the ends to drag on the ground. Burdens of all kinds are strapped on the poles.

Tree, n. The frame-work of a saddle.

U

Under-bit, n. An ear-mark on cattle, signifying ownership, made by cutting out a v-shaped piece from the under side of the ear.

Under-hack, n. An ear-mark on cattle, signifying ownership, made by a slit from the middle to the bottom part of the ear.

Under-half-crop, n. An ear-mark on cattle, signifying ownership, made by cutting away the bottom outside half of the ear.

Under-slope, n. An ear-mark on cattle, signifying ownership, made by cutting away a portion of the ear from the under side to the tip.

V

Vaquero, n. (pronounced "boccario"). A California cow-boy.

Vint, n. A brand signifying that an animal has been sold.

W

War-bag, n. A cow-boy's Saratoga trunk. The bag in which he carries his extra clothes &c.

Wash-out, n. A gully worn in the ground by water from rains or melted snow.

Wrangle-footed, adj. A horse's gait. A mixture of several gaits.

Wrangler, n. See horse-wrangler.
articles.summary: Second installment of the Cow Boy's glossary of range terms (P through W), thanking C. R. Kelsey and Rassie Deffebach for corrections.

articles.text: James Foley, of Bismarck, arrived in Medora last evening.
articles.summary: James Foley of Bismarck arrived in Medora.

articles.text: Harry Tarbell's stray horses were found near Miles City, Tuesday.
articles.summary: Harry Tarbell's strayed horses were found near Miles City.

articles.text: Roberts & Co. are moving their saloon to-day to the old skating rink.
articles.summary: Roberts & Co. moved their saloon into the old skating rink.

articles.text: S. W. Russel, having delivered the N bar cattle, returned to Miles City, Saturday.
articles.summary: S. W. Russel delivered the N bar cattle and returned to Miles City.

articles.text: S.A. Marney, the rustler and proprietor of the Stockgrowers' Journal, was here Saturday.
articles.summary: S. A. Marney of the Stockgrowers' Journal visited Medora.

articles.text: Col. Malone, known everywhere on the line as stock agent of C. M. & St. P., was in Medora Saturday.
articles.summary: Col. Malone, stock agent of the C. M. & St. P. railway, was in Medora.

articles.text: A reliable report from Dickinson states that the crops there were damaged fifty per cent. by the hail Tuesday.
articles.summary: Tuesday's hail reportedly damaged Dickinson crops by fifty percent.

articles.text: Agent Maxwell is death on prairie chickens, for which the guests at the Northern Pacific owe him many thanks.
articles.summary: Railroad agent Maxwell has been supplying the Northern Pacific hotel with prairie chickens.

articles.text: Henry Boice, of the 777 outfit, left Medora, Sunday night, having delivered five hundred cattle, averaging 1021½.
articles.summary: Henry Boice of the 777 outfit delivered 500 cattle at Medora and left.

articles.text: Wilmot Dow and wife arrived from Maine last Sunday evening in company with Mrs. Sewall. They are now at home at the Elkhorn ranch.
articles.summary: Wilmot Dow, his wife and Mrs. Sewall arrived from Maine and are at the Elkhorn ranch.

articles.text: J. G. Ramsey, live-stock broker, of Glendive, was in Medora Saturday. He is working up a good business, having made a number of sales this year.
articles.summary: Glendive live-stock broker J. G. Ramsey visited Medora.

articles.text: Blanks and instructions have been received at the Medora post-office for a money-order business. This will be a great convenience to those desiring to send money away.
articles.summary: The Medora post office received materials to begin a money-order business.

articles.text: The outfits up the river have adopted the very sensible plan of driving their cattle back from the river bottoms and thus preserving the feed. This will increase the quality of the herds ten per cent. next spring.
articles.summary: Outfits up the Little Missouri are driving cattle back from the river bottoms to save the feed.

articles.text: The storm of Tuesday, of which we had merely a touch, did considerable damage at Belfield. Passengers on the train stated that the ground was covered with hail-stones from five to eight inches in circumference.
articles.summary: Tuesday's hailstorm did considerable damage at Belfield, only touching Medora.

articles.text: Joe. Cuskelley, formerly of Little Missouri, and now of Dickinson, came in from the east Tuesday evening. The Cuskelley Bros. have a good herd of cattle in the Killdeer M't's., and their brand will soon appear in the COW BOY.
articles.summary: Joe Cuskelley of Dickinson came in from the east; the Cuskelley Bros. run cattle in the Killdeer Mountains.

articles.text: Orders came from the Marquis Tuesday to begin killing a hundred to a hundred and twenty-five cattle per day. This will set the works running on full time. If the present contract for beef holds permanently, the slaughter-house and cooling rooms will be enlarged.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès ordered his Medora slaughter-house to kill 100 to 125 cattle a day.

articles.text: Joe. Ferris is moving his stock of goods into his new store to-day. The building is completed with the exception of the second story and is the best store-building in Medora. Joe deserves success for his enterprise and will undoubtedly secure it.
articles.summary: Joe Ferris moved his goods into his new store building, called the best in Medora.

articles.text: Geo. W. Reynolds, of Albany, Texas, arrived Friday evening and in company with his brother B. F., who has been here for some time went to Mingusville Saturday. The two may ride down to Stoneville to meet their herd of 4,500, which they will probably locate on Elk creek.
articles.summary: George W. Reynolds of Albany, Texas, arrived and went with his brother B. F. to Mingusville to meet a herd of 4,500.

articles.text: A letter from Dr. J. J. Clemmer, of Cresco, Iowa, shows that he is still enthusiastic over Aberdeen-Angus cattle. He has a calf born last March, that gained a hundred and fifty pounds in forty days on grass alone. The Dr. and G. M. Dell own the Aberdeen-Angus herd in Cave Hills.
articles.summary: Dr. J. J. Clemmer writes of his Aberdeen-Angus cattle; he and G. M. Dell own the herd in the Cave Hills.

articles.text: The flying, lazy E bar outfit have fifteen hundred cattle on Garner creek, for delivery to the Co. Five hundred head will be delivered Aug. 15, five hundred Aug. 22, and five hundred, Sept. 1. The cattle belong to Myers Bros., of Wyoming and come from the same herd that the best lot of cattle killed this year by the Co. came from.
articles.summary: The flying lazy E bar outfit holds 1,500 Myers Bros. cattle on Garner creek for delivery to 'the Co.' in three lots.

articles.text: Following are the arrivals at the Northern Pacific hotel for the last week: Peter H. Pernot, Washington, D. C.; S. W. Russel, Miles City; H. S. Boice, Mingusville; W. H. Sewell, Elkhorn ranch; J. A. Chapman, W. Cushion, Jr., Wellington, Ohio; Wilmot Dow and wife and Mrs. Sewall, Elkhorn ranch; O. B. Jenison, E. R. Jenison, Wapello, Iowa; L. H. Parker, J. A. Knowles. Buffalo, Wyoming,; B. R. Thorpson, Sante Fe, N. M.; Ed. Newton and wife, Medora; James Foley, Bismarck, Geo. Harmon, Mandan.
articles.summary: Weekly register of arrivals at the Northern Pacific hotel, including W. H. Sewell, Wilmot Dow and Mrs. Sewall of the Elkhorn ranch.

articles.text: Wm. Van Driesche returned Tuesday morning from the hunting trip in the Big Horn. The Marquise and party are coming more slowly and will be in Medora in a day or two. The party hunted on the west side of the Big Horn, on the Meteetse river, not going into the Big Horn range. The hunting was good but would have been much better had they gone into the mountains. A number of bear were killed, the Marquise getting an old bear and two cubs and William securing a fine silver-tip. Elk were not very numerous nor were mountain sheep. Antelope and small game were very plentiful. Mountain trout abounded in every stream, averaging from one to three pounds. Other parties that had gone into the mountains reported large numbers of bear, elk and mountain sheep. The Marquise delayed a day or two in hopes that she might get a mountain sheep. Vic and Frank Smith expect to start on another hunting expedition immediately, probably going into the Big Horn M't's. Tommy Skinner and Sweet will return to Medora with the stock. Altogether the trip according to William, was one extremely full of pleasure.
articles.summary: William Van Driesche returned from the Marquise de Morès's Big Horn hunting trip, on which she killed a bear and two cubs; the Marquise is due back shortly.

articles.text: Superintendent Green stopped off in Medora Tuesday night.
articles.summary: Superintendent Green stopped off in Medora.

articles.text: Mrs. and Paul Pierce, wife and son of the Governor and Col. and Mrs. Steele, went west Tuesday to visit the National Park.
articles.summary: The governor's wife and son, Mrs. and Paul Pierce, and Col. and Mrs. Steele went west to Yellowstone National Park.

articles.text: Fred Banan returned yesterday morn from Fort Keogh, where he has completed his term of service in the U. S. army. We welcome him back to Medora as making one of a class of citizens which we need.
articles.summary: Fred Banan returned to Medora from Fort Keogh after completing his army service.

articles.text: This season, about 2,500 cattle will be shipped from Medora. On account of the difficulty of shipping here the most of the cattle tributary to Medora will be shipped from Mingusville or Dickinson.
articles.summary: About 2,500 cattle will be shipped from Medora this season; most area cattle will go from Mingusville or Dickinson.

articles.text: The first sixteen cars of tea from the steamship Isabel passed through Medora last evening. There are two hundred car loads in the lot. The tea will be taken from Portland to St. Paul in 160 hours.
articles.summary: The first sixteen cars of a 200-car tea shipment from the steamship Isabel passed through Medora.

articles.text:
Monday morning our citizens were startled by the news that Peter Birch had been shot. As luck would have it Dr. Robarts happened to come in on the east-bound train and, taking charge of the case, found that the ball had gone through the biceps muscle, entered his side under his arm and going around under the skin to within an inch and a half of the backbone, where it emerged. The account as told by Peter, was as follows, the other participators in the affair having gone to Mandan as witnesses at court, only his side can be learned. Peter states that at about half past twelve o'clock Monday morning he was in Bob. Roberts' saloon, in company with Roberts and Wm. Jones. That Roberts suggested playing a joke on some one in MacDonald's restaurant by cutting down the hammock in which he was sleeping. Peter started with Bob to the restaurant and the hammock was cut down. Bob asked Peter to take the knife back to the saloon and Peter started back in company with Jones. The latter asked Peter who was running the restaurant now and Peter told him that he had been cooking there for about a week. This led to what Peter thought was playful banter when Jones struck him on the forehead with the but of his revolver. His eyes were blinded with blood but he attempted to ward off other blows, when Jones shot. Attempting then to run, he was struck several more times on the back of the head, there being eight gashes extending to the skull. Peter did not know he was shot until the morning when he found his arm covered with blood and examining it, found he was shot. He further added that he was perfectly sober, only having two drinks early in the evening. This is one side of the case and we will gladly publish the other. We have few comments to make, as there were no witnesses. Both men have reputations for peaceable dispositions. Jones is well liked and every one is anxious to hear his side of the story. Peter is as harmless a man as ever lived, he being his own worst enemy. The principal point we make is the one so often mentioned in the COW BOY, that of carrying revolvers in town. Every shooting affray we know of has been caused by whiskey, coupled with the senseless custom of "packing a gun." We have many times mentioned our opinion and cannot sufficiently condemn a practice that no one can say has ever resulted in good and many times results fatally.

[Since writing the above, Sheriff Harmon arrived in Medora with a warrant for the arrest of Peter Birch. Probably for assault and battery. Jones was arrested at Mandan and released on his own recognizance. Sheriff Harmon returned this morning to Mandan. Birch was unable to be moved.]
articles.summary: Peter Birch was shot and beaten in Medora early Monday, by his account by Wm. Jones; the paper condemns carrying revolvers in town, and Sheriff Harmon later came with a warrant for Birch.
